replacement: 'No, indeed,' I replied, 'it was the same man who told Phoenix. He was a little fellow who never wore shoes, Aristodemus of the deme of Cydathenaeum. He had been at Agathon's feast, and I think that in those days no one admired Socrates more devotedly. I have also asked Socrates about parts of his account, and Socrates confirmed them.' 'Then,' said Glaucon, 'let us have the story again. Is the road to Athens not made for conversation?' So we walked and talked about the speeches on love. And that is why, as I said at the start, I am quite ready to do as you ask, and I will go over them again if you like. For I take the greatest pleasure in speaking about philosophy, or hearing others speak of it, quite apart from the benefit. But when I hear other talk, especially the talk of you rich men and traders, it annoys me, and I pity you, my companions, because you think you are accomplishing something when you are really accomplishing nothing. I suppose you pity me in return, and think me an unfortunate creature, and very likely you are right. But what you merely think about me, I know about you. That is the difference.

replacement: Take what we are doing now, drinking, singing and talking. These actions are in themselves neither good nor evil. They turn out one way or the other according to how they are done. Done well, they are good, and done wrongly, they are evil. In the same way, not every love is noble and worthy of praise, but only the love that has a noble purpose. The Love who is the child of the common Aphrodite is common in his very nature and has no discrimination. He is the love felt by the lower sort of men, who are apt to love women as well as youths, and who love the body rather than the soul. The objects of this love are the most foolish people, for it desires only to reach its goal and never considers reaching it nobly, so it does good and evil quite indiscriminately. The goddess who is his mother is much younger than the other, and she was born from the union of male and female and shares in both. But the child of the heavenly Aphrodite comes from a mother in whose birth the female has no part. She comes from the male only. This is the love of youths, and since the goddess is older, there is no wantonness in her. Those inspired by this love turn to the male, and delight in the one who is braver and more intelligent by nature. Anyone can recognize the pure enthusiasts of this love by the very character of their attachments.
